newsitem.title: UK: UK Pop industry on track for record year.
newsitem.headline: UK Pop industry on track for record year.

text.p: British pop music is on track for a record year in 1997, recalling the glory days of the Sixties when the Beatles ruled the world.
The Spice Girls, a feisty quintet who boast Margaret Thatcher as their role model, have gone to Number One in the United States with their first single, a feat never achieved by the Beatles.
Sales of pop albums in Britain have broken through the 200 million barrier for the first time and analysts on Wednesday forecast that the UK market is headed for 10 percent growth this year.
Latest figures from the British Phonographic Industry (BPI), pop music's trade umbrella, showed sales up 6.1 percent last year. The market for singles has grown to its highest level since 1982.
The timing could not be better -- next week the pop business picks the Brit Awards for its top stars. The Spice Girls, who have topped the charts in 31 countries, are expected to sweep the board.
The ebullience of music companies' pony-tailed executives is for once justified in an industry which generates more money for the economy than shipbuilding or electronic components.
A research report for The National Music Council estimated that the recording industry was now worth 2.5 billion pounds ($4 billion) and generated 11,000 jobs.
The industry is optimistic about the future. "There is a very strong lineup of albums due out this year," said BPI spokeswoman Sarah Roberts.
"We had an excellent year which was much better than expected. Our gross is better than the United States, Japan and Germany. We are the fourth biggest," she said.
Chris Page, share analyst at Goldman Sachs, agreed: "It is looking to be one of the better markets globally. We are looking for growth of 10 percent in units and revenue."
In the latest Goldman Sachs review of the international pop industry, he singled out Britain as a major source of global music.
World music sales now total more than $40 billion annually after rapid growth over the past decade. Growth slowed markedly last year but booming Britain bucked the gloomy trend.

David Hughes, director of external affairs at EMI Records, echoed many other executives with his enthusiastic assessment of the industry, whose Britpop stars like Oasis are highly marketable worldwide.
"The climate for UK artists abroad now is getting better and better. In the last couple of years we have had Blur, Radiohead, Supergrass and Eternal. All have new albums this year," he said.
"We are very upbeat for the year going forward. The world will always listen to what Britain has to offer. The Beatles started that," he added.
Martin Talbot of Music Week magazine agreed that the industry's ability to talk up a storm had some weight behind it this time.
"It is looking pretty amazing at the moment. The Spice Girls really filled a gap in the market. They are empowering for young girls," he said.
"We have had a pretty rough time in the United States. The Spice Girls were the first British number one in America for 18 months. That is a pretty long time."
He said British artists were also big sellers in fast expanding markets like Australia and Asia and were establishing a niche in eastern Europe.
"The music scene is far more vibrant in the UK than it has been for a long time. The industry is making the kind of music people want to listen to."($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
